# Assessing diet and talking to patients

> *Advice is only as good as the assessment behind it. We cover how to find out what a patient eats
> (assessment methods, the diet history and reading a food label), how to interpret what the history
> shows, including screening for malnutrition, and how to open a brief conversation about change without
> doing harm.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Choose a fit-for-purpose dietary assessment method, and name the characteristic bias of the 24-hour
  recall, the food-frequency questionnaire and the food diary.
- Take a structured diet history, and explain why the drinks question is especially informative in a Singapore
  diet.
- Read a Nutrition Information Panel per 100 g or 100 ml, and grade a drink with Nutri-Grade.
- Link a diet pattern to its likely surpluses and shortfalls, and interpret BMI and waist
  circumference against the Asian cut-offs.
- Recognise malnutrition risk and eating-disorder red flags, and refer instead of advising
  restriction.
- Open a brief counselling conversation by assessing first and advising one change with permission,
  in plain language.
:::

## Assessing diet and talking to patients at a glance {#sec-overview}

Knowing what people should eat (see the [*What a healthy diet looks like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd)
chapter) is useful only once the clinician knows what a patient eats now: a diet cannot be counselled
before it has been assessed. The tool is the **diet history**, a structured conversation about what a
patient usually eats and drinks. The same short conversation that surfaces food also surfaces
drinking, activity, sleep and stress. A diet history is therefore one branch of a whole lifestyle
history, and the skill transfers to the rest of it.

Medical students and recent graduates report gaps in the knowledge, skills and confidence to give
nutrition care, including talking to patients about food [@crowley2019]. The goal at this stage is competent first contact:
take a basic history, read a label, flag the likely problems and open the conversation. Specialist
assessment and a therapeutic plan lie beyond first contact; where a plan turns detailed or
restrictive, you recognise it and refer.

::: {.callout-note}
## From one's own plate to a patient's
A diet history has the same structure whether the plate is one's own or a patient's: a typical day,
the drinks, the portions, who cooks. The difference is the patient, who may not want to talk about it
and will only tell you what you ask.
:::

## Assessing dietary intake {#sec-assess-intake}

### Dietary assessment methods and their biases {#sec-methods}

No single method of dietary assessment is best, so the choice is the one that fits the purpose. Each
of the three standard tools carries a characteristic bias [@measurementToolkitDiet]. The comparison
below depends on three terms:

Habitual intake
: What a person usually eats over months, as opposed to on any one day.

Recall bias
: Error in reported intake that arises because the report depends on memory.

Reactivity
: Eating differently because intake is being recorded.

| Method | What it is | Strength | Characteristic bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24-hour recall | "Tell me everything you ate and drank yesterday." | Quick, low burden for the patient | One day is not necessarily a usual day: intake varies widely from day to day, and the method relies on memory (recall bias). Several non-consecutive recalls estimate habitual intake far better. |
| Food-frequency questionnaire | A checklist: how often, over months, do you eat X? | Captures the habitual pattern; low burden | Best for ranking people (high vs low), not for measuring exact quantities; portion estimation is rough. |
| Food diary | The patient records everything as they eat it, for several days | The most detail; no memory error | High burden; reactivity; and people under-report the "bad" items. |

Two caveats apply to all three methods. First, self-reported intake shows systematic
**under-reporting**: people leave out or shrink the less-flattering foods and portions, and
under-reporting is greater at higher body weight [@measurementToolkitDiet]. Second, the remedy is the
manner of asking, not suspicion: a question should not invite the "right" answer (see
[Taking a diet history](#sec-diet-history)). For a first clinic visit the fit-for-purpose choice is
usually a short structured history, which is a guided 24-hour recall widened with "is that typical?".

### Taking a diet history {#sec-diet-history}

A diet history is a structured conversation, not an interrogation. Walk through a typical day from
waking to sleeping, then probe the most informative areas: meal pattern and skipping, drinks, snacks, how
often they eat out or *tapau* (buy takeaway), portion sizes, who shops and cooks, and supplements.
Keep it conversational, and let the facts come out instead of firing questions.

Locally, the most useful single probe is drinks. Sugary drinks (*kopi* and *teh* with condensed
milk, *bandung*, bubble tea, canned soft drinks) were the single biggest source of sugar in the 2022
National Nutrition Survey, about half of all sugar eaten [@mohNNS2022], and they are the question most often skipped. The drinks probe also
folds in a routine, non-judgemental question about alcohol.

Try the history below: click the questions you would ask and watch the picture build, and notice what
you miss if you never ask what she drinks.

<div data-island="diet-history" data-src="/diagrams/diet-history.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-tip}
## The most useful question is often the one not asked
People rarely volunteer their drinks, their snacks or their true portions, not to deceive but because
they feel these "don't count". Ask specifically, with everyday comparisons ("how big, a *rice bowl*? two
scoops?"), and you uncover far more than an open "so, how's your diet?" ever will.
:::

### Reading a food label {#sec-food-label}

A packaged food or drink carries a **Nutrition Information Panel**, the nutrient table quoted per
serving and per 100 g or 100 ml. Its trap is the serving size. The per-serving figure may describe a
small or unrealistic serving: a bottle labelled "2.5 servings" hides how much sugar a person drinks
when they finish it in one go. The per-100 g or per-100 ml column is the one to check, because it
compares products fairly. The ingredient list adds one more signal: it is ordered by weight, so sugar
near the top, under any of its many names, is a warning. (The policy behind labels and the wider food
environment is in the [*What a healthy diet looks like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd) chapter.)

### Nutri-Grade: front-of-pack grading of drinks {#sec-nutri-grade}

Nutri-Grade, Singapore's front-of-pack mark for drinks (see the
[*Why nutrition matters*](01-why-nutrition-matters.qmd) chapter), turns the label into a one-glance
judgement. It grades a beverage A to D by sugar per 100 ml (A ≤1 g, B >1–5 g, C >5–10 g, D >10 g).
A high saturated-fat content then downgrades it, so a low-sugar but creamy drink still cannot
reach an A. Grades C and D must display the mark, and grade D cannot be advertised. Since 30 December 2023 the mark has also covered freshly-prepared drinks such as *kopi*, *teh* and bubble tea, although small sellers (revenue of S$1 million or less and fewer than 10 outlets) are exempt; pre-packaged drinks have carried it since 30 December 2022 [@hpbNutriGrade]. That reach makes "grade
your usual drink, then pick one swap" an authentic local exercise:

<div data-island="nutri-grade" data-src="/diagrams/nutri-grade.yml"></div>

Nutri-Grade works as a nudge, not a verdict. In a randomised trial of the label, shoppers bought
drinks with less sugar (about 1.5 g less per serving), but the label alone did not improve the overall
quality of their basket [@nutriGradeRCT2023]. A grade influences one choice; it does not change the whole diet. It
also grades only drinks, on two nutrients: an "A" drink is not a licence, and Nutri-Grade says nothing
about solid food.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out: start with the drink
In a Singapore diet history, the drink is usually the most useful thing to swap. Four swaps make it concrete:

- *kopi-o kosong* or *teh-o kosong* (grade A) instead of the sweetened default;
- *siu dai* (less sweet) or *kosong* (no sugar) when ordering;
- water instead of the bundled soft drink;
- whole fruit instead of a pressed juice.

One realistic swap the patient agrees to is more useful than a lecture on all of them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient's 24-hour recall describes a light, healthy day. Why can't that be taken as her usual diet?
One recalled day is not necessarily a usual day: intake varies widely from day to day, and the account
depends on memory (recall bias). Self-reported intake is also systematically under-reported, because
people leave out or shrink the less-flattering foods and portions. Asking "is that typical?" widens
the recall towards habitual intake, and asking specifically about drinks, snacks and portions, with
everyday comparisons, uncovers what people do not volunteer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has switched all her drinks to grade A. Why might her diet still need work?
Nutri-Grade grades only drinks, and only on sugar and saturated fat, so it says nothing about the solid
food she eats. In a randomised trial the label moved drink purchases towards less sugar but did not
improve the overall quality of shoppers' baskets. A grade influences one choice but not the whole diet,
so the rest of the history still needs reading.
:::

## Interpreting the diet history {#sec-history-problems}

### Likely surpluses and shortfalls {#sec-likely-problems}

A history is useful only when it points to the likely surpluses and shortfalls in the patient's
pattern. National data show that most residents exceed the sodium recommendation and that very little
of the staple eaten is wholegrain [@mohNNS2022], so the local pattern is predictable. Three surpluses
recur, each with familiar sources:

- sodium, from instant noodles, soup bases and sauces on everything;
- free sugars, from the sugary drinks above;
- saturated fat, from coconut gravy, fried food and fatty or processed meat.

The shortfalls follow the same pattern: wholegrains, fibre, fruit and vegetables, and in some groups
calcium or iron. You are not calculating nutrient intakes; you are reading a pattern and naming, in
plain terms, the two or three things worth shifting.

### Anthropometry and malnutrition screening {#sec-both-tails}

**Anthropometry** (body measurements such as weight, height and waist circumference) adds objective
measurements to the history. BMI classifies weight-for-height (see the
[*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd#sec-measuring) chapter), but its thresholds are not universal.
Singapore uses lower Asian cut-offs, because cardiometabolic risk rises at a lower BMI in Asian
populations than the international thresholds assume [@sgObesityBMI]:

| Category | Asian cut-off, used in Singapore | International cut-off |
|---|---|---|
| Overweight | BMI ≥23 kg/m² | BMI ≥25 kg/m² |
| Obese | BMI ≥27.5 kg/m² | BMI ≥30 kg/m² |

A waist circumference of ≥90 cm in men or ≥80 cm in women flags excess central (visceral) fat [@sgObesityBMI]. BMI is
a screen, not a verdict: it misses body composition (a muscular person, or an older person who has
lost muscle), so it is read alongside the history, not instead of it.

Malnutrition covers excess (overnutrition) as well as deficit (undernutrition), the two tails of the
same range, and the commoner instinct is to look only at excess. Some patients are undernourished: an
unwell older adult who has lost weight
and appetite, or someone eating alone and skipping meals. A validated tool such as the **Malnutrition
Universal Screening Tool (MUST)**, which combines BMI, recent unplanned weight loss and any acute
illness stopping intake, flags this risk and triggers a referral pathway [@bapenMUST].

Unplanned weight loss earns its place in MUST for a physiological reason. A sustained energy deficit,
worsened by illness, drives catabolism of **lean body mass** (muscle and organ protein) as well as fat
(see prolonged fasting in the [*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-starvation)
chapter). The loss of that functional tissue erodes strength, immunity and recovery. A falling weight
is therefore a red flag even when the BMI still reads "normal", which is why MUST scores recent loss
independently of BMI. At this stage you recognise when MUST applies and refer; you do not need to
score and manage it (see the [*Undernutrition & malnutrition*](undernutrition-malnutrition.qmd)
chapter for the recognition and management of the malnourished patient).

::: {.callout-important}
## Always consider undernutrition
"Lower on the scale is better" is a dangerous default. Before you suggest anyone eat less, ask whether
the problem is in fact that they are eating too little, and whether weight talk is safe at all (see
[Do no harm](#sec-do-no-harm)).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can a doctor in Singapore anticipate a patient's likely surpluses before the history is finished?
National data show that most residents exceed the sodium recommendation and that very little of the
staple eaten is wholegrain, and the local food pattern (sauces and soup bases, sugary drinks, coconut
gravy and fried food) makes sodium, free sugars and saturated fat the predictable surpluses. The
history then confirms which apply to this patient, so the task is reading a pattern and naming two or
three things worth shifting, not calculating nutrient intakes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an older patient has had unplanned weight loss over three months, but her BMI still reads "normal". Why does the loss still matter?
MUST scores recent unplanned weight loss independently of BMI, because the loss itself does the harm.
A sustained energy deficit, worsened by illness, breaks down lean body mass (muscle and organ protein)
as well as fat, and losing that functional tissue erodes strength, immunity and recovery. A falling
weight is therefore a red flag while the BMI still reads normal; the response at this stage is to
recognise the risk and refer.
:::

## Brief counselling {#sec-conversation}

### The 5 A's: assess and advise {#sec-first-moves}

Knowing the food is half the job; the other half is the conversation, which has its own structure.
The widely recommended scaffold for brief counselling is the **5 A's**, five steps that run in
sequence [@fiveAsNutrition]:

::: {.flow}
1. Assess
2. Advise
3. Agree
4. Assist
5. Arrange
:::

The full cycle, and the motivational-interviewing skills behind it, are in the
[*Behaviour-change counselling*](behaviour-change-counselling.qmd) chapter. The opening steps, assess
and advise, are the focus at first contact. Assessing means finding out what the patient
eats and what they are ready to change, without judgement; it is the diet history above. Advising
means offering one concrete, realistic step, with permission: "Would it be alright if I shared one
idea about your drinks?" earns a hearing, and an unasked-for lecture does not.

Two rules carry most of the weight. Ask before advising, because permission turns advice into a
conversation. Use plain language: "sugary drinks", not "free sugars exceeding ten percent of energy".
Counselling in this respectful, motivational-interviewing style can produce small, mostly short-term
improvements in some health behaviours, such as drinking and physical activity; for diet specifically
the evidence is of low quality [@frost2018mi].

### Do no harm: eating-disorder red flags and screening {#sec-do-no-harm}

Food, weight and "clean eating" talk can trigger or worsen disordered eating. Behavioural
weight-management programmes do not raise eating-disorder symptoms for most adults (on average they
ease slightly), but a small minority develop new symptoms, so vigilance still matters
[@jebeile2023edrisk]. A do-no-harm reflex therefore belongs at first contact, before any advice to
restrict. The red flags to listen for are:

- skipping meals to "make up" for eating;
- guilt or secrecy around food;
- a driven pursuit of thinness;
- weight talk that feels charged.

When something flags, a brief screen such as **SCOFF** (five questions on vomiting, loss of control,
recent weight loss, feeling fat, and food dominating life) raises or lowers suspicion. Two measures
describe how well a screen performs: its **sensitivity**, the proportion of people with the condition
whom it correctly flags, and its **specificity**, the proportion without it whom it correctly clears.
SCOFF was first validated in young women with anorexia or bulimia [@scoffMorgan1999]; pooled across
25 validation studies, its sensitivity is about 0.86 and its specificity about 0.83 [@kutzScoff2020]. SCOFF is a screen, not a diagnosis: a positive result means ask
more and consider referral, and a negative result does not exclude an eating disorder. The safe
response at this stage is the same either way: do not prescribe restriction into a possible eating
disorder; be supportive, and refer.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why open with "Would it be alright if I shared one idea about your drinks?" instead of "You need to cut down on sugar"?
Asking permission turns advice into a conversation, so the idea that follows earns a hearing; an
unasked-for lecture does not. The first version also narrows the advice to one target, the drinks,
where the second is a broad instruction. Respectful, permission-first counselling can bring small, short-term
changes in some health behaviours, though the evidence that it changes diet is of low quality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient asking for a diet screens negative on SCOFF but mentions skipping meals to make up for eating. Why doesn't the negative screen settle it?
SCOFF is a screen, not a diagnosis. With a sensitivity of about 0.86 it misses some people who have an
eating disorder, so a negative result does not exclude one, and compensatory meal-skipping is itself a
red flag. The safe response is the same either way: do not prescribe restriction into a possible
eating disorder; be supportive, and refer.
:::

## How should a first nutrition conversation start? {#sec-close}

It starts with asking, not advising. First contact done well has five parts, in roughly this order:

1. Take a quick, structured history, and make sure to ask about the drinks.
2. Read the label with the patient: check per 100 ml, grade the drink, name one swap.
3. Check the findings for undernutrition as well as excess, using the Asian BMI cut-offs and
   recognising when a screening tool is indicated.
4. Say one useful, permission-first sentence.
5. When the picture is complex or restrictive, or a red flag shows, recognise the boundary and refer.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Nutri-Grade is useful in practice because it now reaches many of the freshly-prepared drinks people
actually buy, such as bubble tea and coffee from the larger chains, so "grade your drink" is a real
exercise and not a supermarket abstraction [@hpbNutriGrade]. The National Nutrition Survey shows what to expect before the patient
says a word: high sodium, sweet drinks, refined staples and too little wholegrain [@mohNNS2022]. The
whole approach also fits the national direction of preventive care: screening and a short
conversation at first contact, then referral where needed, instead of waiting for disease.

## Practise: weight gain and bubble tea {#sec-case}

A 24-year-old office worker, overweight by the Asian cut-off, has gained weight over the past year
and asks you for "a diet". Take a history, ask about the drinks, open the conversation with
permission, and stay alert for the signal that this is not a weight-loss conversation at all. Your
choices branch the case.
